title: Defending AI - Quality Matters - Distance Matters
author: Riitoken
selftext:
**Defending AI — Quality Matters. Distance Matters.**

I’ve worked in the game industry multiple times. One thing that was completely normal was seeing an artist drawing on the main monitor while reference images were open on a side screen or spread across books on the desk. That artist was still making something new, but they were clearly using existing work as visual input.

Nobody acted like that was some outrageous moral crime. It was just part of the process.

That is why I think a lot of the anti-AI rhetoric is weak.

For images, the issue is not whether reference existed. Reference has always existed. The issue is **distance**.

If the final work is too close to some original piece, that is a problem. If it is sufficiently transformed, legally defensible, and clearly its own final result, then that is the standard that should matter. Humans are judged that way. AI should be judged that way too.

And yes, “distance” can be subjective around the edges. That is also true for human-made work. That does not destroy the principle. It just means the principle requires judgment.

For me, it comes down to two things:

**Quality and distance.**

If I am building a game, my job is to use the best images, music, sound, and assets I can legally obtain in order to make the best game I can. My first obligation is to the player experience.

Not to random moral debt collectors on the internet.  
Not to people demanding that I use a specific workflow so they can feel righteous.  
Not to critics who think a dev must structure their whole project around somebody else’s politics.

You owe players an honest effort to make a good game.  
You owe the law compliance.  
You owe the work quality.

That is enough.

Music is no different.

Human musicians have always borrowed from other musicians. Style, phrasing, rhythm, tone, production, genre conventions, melodic resemblance — this has always existed. That is not some shocking new corruption introduced by AI. That is the history of music.

So when somebody throws out the word **“thief”** just because AI was used, my view is simple:

Show the evidence.

Show that the output is unlawfully close to a protected work.  
Show that the distance is insufficient.  
Show something concrete.

If you cannot do that, then you are not making a serious argument. You are making an accusation.

Same thing with the word **“slop.”**

Sure, low-quality AI exists.  
Low-quality human art exists too.  
Low-quality music exists.  
Low-quality code exists.  
Low-quality games exist.

“Slop” is not an argument against AI. It is an argument against bad work.

So yes, I agree that low quality is bad. The real question is whether the asset is good enough to serve the game.

If a human can do better, great.  
If they cannot do better, or cannot do it at the needed speed, budget, or style, then moral posturing does not solve anything.

A developer is not obligated to choose the slower, harder, or more expensive path just to satisfy ideological spectators.

For me, the real test is simple:

Is the output good?  
Is it legal?  
Is it sufficiently distant from protected originals?  
Does it serve the game?

That is the standard.

Everything else is mostly noise.

**FARCRAFT** uses some AI images and some AI music/themes. My position is simple: I will use the best images and audio I can legally obtain, because my first obligation is to make the best game I can.

The game is the point.

Not every splash image.  
Not every piece of promo art.  
Not every menu track.  
Not every texture or visual element the player will barely see for one percent of the experience.

The player experience is the center.

As for audio, FARCRAFT is about humans in space 200 years in the future. I built an in-game radio station, **WKFR**, inspired by the same broad idea that made radio so memorable in other games. But WKFR has one huge advantage: it is not limited to one narrow historical style. It can play different moods, genres, and fictional broadcasts that fit the world of FARCRAFT.

That flexibility matters.

If a tool helps me build that world better, and I can use it lawfully, I will use it.

That is not theft.

That is development.

replies.author: sammoga123
replies.body:
Well, it's the only way, you know how computers work?

Living beings function with a biological brain, with hormones and electrical impulses.

The latter does happen in a processor, but ultimately they're just transistors turning on and off like switches. That's the basic principle. It's a giant calculator where a processor performs billions of on/off cycles continuously to do what it needs to do.

A biological brain is more complex than that. And that's what the engineers tried to replicate; you can't compare a chemical reaction to a partial derivative, for example.

Probability has always existed; things discovered and accomplished by a human being were not actually the work of just one human being. There were people before who tried, made mistakes, and surely suffered or died to "prove" something.

In the end, haven't you ever stopped to think about how on earth those cooking recipes were created? What are the chances that if you combine this with that and follow this process for this amount of time, it will result in something delicious to eat? Surely many people who are no longer with us were trying that, cooking times, ingredients, etc. After all, if you simplify it mathematically, it ultimately comes down to probability.

The fact that a computer has to process information differently to try to learn, versus a humanity with billions of years of evolution, well, what can I say? Besides, I find it ironic that you used the example of perfumery when there's nothing electronically to transmit scent.

Furthermore, have you ever wondered what the combination is for, for example, creating music with all the instruments we know? Certainly, there's a limit to the number of musical notes and ranges, but in the end, coincidences happen, inspiration exists, because you, as a human being with years on Earth, surely have tastes, and that will always affect your perspective on life.

replies.author: Riitoken
replies.body:
You said it again.  You're agreeing that humans and AI are influenced by other sources.  But you're complaining that AI has a super-power beyond what a human can do.  You're complaining about the "scale" of influence.

So, in the regard, AI is a savant - perhaps an idiot savant. 

Right now, today, this very second, I would replace any AI asset in my game with a human sourced assets - provided the quality is equal or better, and the style is what I want (I choose my game style not an artist).

Why is that not likely to happen?  Because of humans are slow'er - and they have feelings.

As a solodev, it's utterly fantastic that I can farm an AI asset (image or audio) and the AI never complains, never asks me for a raise (I have subscriptions).  It's like an extension of myself - obeys all my commands as well as it can.  And it keeps trying until I'm happy.

That's the kind of employee I want - now what creative person will agree to those terms?

I'm a solodev, trying to bring a game to market.  AI as increased my motivation to keep going.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
You're confining it to a single artist, every professional artist in the world works this way and has always worked that way. Now imagine they all needed to pay to use work as inspiration or reference. I trained as a digital designer at uni, backup work as in gathering data, was the largest and most important aspect of my course. Studying the work of other artists and creatives was also a key element. This is how all professional artists are trained.

On top of that we are all surrounded by the work of others every minute of the day. Every single object in the world is someone's design work or creative concept and our brains take all that in and use those concepts for our own ideas and concepts, consciously or unconsciously. Every working artist today is where they are because of the people that came before. AI works in a very similar way as it's trained on concepts.

AI is also transformative, if an AI is closely producing the work it was trained on then it has been overtrained on that particular concept which is not what people want from AI models because it makes them inflexible.

Yes data is scrapped but apart from a couple of cases it's all publicly available data. You know companies like Google and every other search engine scrape all that same data online and make huge profits from doing so too right? Scraping publicly available data is not illegal. 

Copyright cases are absolutely relevant because this is what people use to argue that training AI on publicly available images is against copyright but it isn't . If an AI produced an image that was close enough to an existing work, as in colors, concept, composition etc then it would fall under general copyright law like every other image.

Not all AI models are the same, many are trained on public domain data. Also some of these large companies you're complaining about such as Adobe for example, own the rights to massive datasets so they don't need to train on public data. The same as if Disney trained an AI model they wouldn't need public data either. Their models would also be closed source and in the case of Disney, more than likely not even available to the public.

People can argue until the end of time about what they think is morally or ethically correct but that's not based around any facts or laws or even right and wrong, they are just concepts that can differ from person to person.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
AI is trained on concepts. Use a thought experiment like this, if you had grown up in dark room with zero concept of the outside world, and someone asked you to draw a dog you wouldn't be able to. However if someone showed you five images of a dog and they were all huskies, your concept of dogs would be that they all look like a husky. This is the same for AI which is why diverse training data is required.

AI Image gen models for example don't store image data, at least not in the way some people imagine. Using the first Stable Diffusion model as an example, it was just a few gigs in size and could be run locally but was trained on roughly 2.3 billion images. Only a percentage of those would be art too, many would just be photos.

This also ties into the silly idea some people have that artists should be credited or paid. Even if an artist had 100 images in the data set that would be something like 0.000004% of the overall content.

Copyright around AI is still up in air as a lot of lawmakers are still unable to decide on it. It changes from country to country and even state to state in the US. AI can absolutely be used to infringe on IP but that's also different to copyright. If someone is selling images of the modern Mickey Mouse or a Marvel hero then Disney can make a claim against them whether AI is used or not. That means technically if a model can produce images of famous IP characters for example then this could be used as a case of IP infringements. Even then this is often just one company bullying a smaller company into submission. In reality it should be the end user that is doing the infringment because they are the ones actually producing the images.

Really it would be a bit like Disney suing a social media platform because it gives people the ability to upload copyrighted or IP infringing images and the platform is profiting from it.

These kind of cases are not really a precedent for anything right now because there's so much inaction and confusion around the legalities of AI. Mainly because AI gen has progressed at an extremely fast rate. Even just with AI image gen we've gone from pixelated messes to images indistinguishable from real photos and art in just the space of a few years.

replies.author: sammoga123
replies.body:
Mathematics will never understand anything; they are basically representations of concepts from reality.

They understand and associate a concept because there are things that are repeated. For example, an apple—we all know that an apple has a somewhat rounded shape with indentations facing downwards and is usually red, yellow, or green. You will never normally see a purple apple.

And well, in the end, an electronic device displays images in a pixel matrix; the pixels are governed by an RGB combination. That is, each pixel has 3 sub-levels of 3 colors: red, green, and blue. If I remember correctly, that intensity is normally 0 (for black) and 256 (for white), the intermediate ones usually give intensity of that color.

So we actually have 5 colors: red, green, blue, black, and white. And if you know anything about color theory, you know that combining any two colors results in another color. Now imagine those 5 colors. The intensity and variability of colors is very extensive, and I'm only talking about a single pixel.

Depending on the quality and aspect ratio of an image, it can be made up of billions of pixels. The AI then analyzes each of those pixels in every image of the dataset. What is the probability that this pixel with this exact color combination is more likely to appear in subsequent pixels? And how long is the matrix that makes up that combination to form "something" that has "shape" within what is supposed to be "something"?

Yes, I think it's too complex to analyze and think about, but basically that's how AI "generates" (hence the name "generative AI") works.

replies.author: sammoga123
replies.body:
You cannot consider AI learning a "theft", just as you cannot consider homeopathy "poison", because, viewed in this way, homeopathy seems somewhat similar to AI.

If you understand the principle of homeopathy, which is basically diluting a dangerous substance thousands of times to supposedly activate its "healing properties," AI ultimately works similarly. It doesn't store anything, but obviously, if something appears frequently, it will tend to remember it. It's like knowing that the Eiffel Tower is in Paris, France; we all know that, and obviously, AI will correlate that the building belongs to France, more specifically to Paris. It doesn't store anything; these are just correlations. The model's weights are relative to the storage size of these correlations, not to the dataset's actual information.

And I haven't even touched on the legal aspects. I'm an engineer, so I don't know much about law, but I do know that there are terms and conditions that nobody reads. Basically, everyone agrees that the data they upload to these sites is global and licensed for free, so that both the company and anyone else can use that toilet paper data if they want. If you don't want to accept that and other terms (like the fact that what you're buying digitally is ultimately just a "license" that you can't even leave to others as an inheritance when you die), then don't accept them. But you won't be able to use the site, the social network, or practically anything else.

comments.author: kmillsom
comments.body:
Blooms Taxonomy of the Cognitive Domain is a model to visualise the different levels of cognition involved in various cognitive activities. 

It has undergone a few reformations since its first publication. One of these includes replacing the term “synthesis” with “creativity”. 

I have always preferred Synthesis. Very little of what we do as humans is pure, blue-sky creation. 99.99% of ‘new’ ideas are born from our experience with existing concepts. I only allow the .001% for products of insanity or divine intervention, because those aside, we are absolutely products of our environment. 

In many cases, it is even more intentional than that. A new idea is very often the conscious amalgamation of several existing concepts. “What if we had that thing, but combined it with this thing?”

So AI is doing nothing different, it is just doing it much faster and over a much wider range of source material. In that regard, it’s not inhuman, it’s superhuman. 

Where it is inhuman is at the level of judgment. “AI slop” is what happens when the LLM is deployed to do that synthesis, and then the LLM is relied upon to determine what is good. AI cannot do this reliably. It cannot know what will land with a human audience.
